Subject: Denis, we need to talk about the building

Denis,

I have tried to write this several times, and each time I get too angry to finish. I am going to try again because you need to understand what this has done to me, and because, even now, I want us to find a way through it.

On Thursday at six in the morning, I was shaping baguettes when a stranger came into my shop with a camera. He was a photographer from the agency. He told me you had said I was okay with him being there.

I had no idea what he was talking about.

That is how I found out you were putting Papa’s building on the market. Not from you. From a stranger standing in my bakery while I was working. Karine had to calm me down. Afterward, I found the listing myself on Centris: $1,150,000.

Do you understand how humiliating that was? To be the last person to know about something that could change my whole life, and to find out in front of my employee? Someone I had never met arrived knowing something about my own building that my brother had not bothered to tell me.

And why did he think I had agreed? I want you to explain that to me. I had not agreed to photographs. I had not agreed to a listing. I had not even been told there was going to be one.

After Maman’s funeral, you called me and said, “No rush, we decide together.” I remember those words. Since she died in February, there has been so much to deal with, and I believed that at least this was something we would handle together. The estate was settled in August. The building is half yours and half mine. How did we go from “we decide together” to an agent sending a photographer into my shop without a call from you?

I am furious with you, Denis. I will not pretend otherwise just to make this email easier to read. You should have called me yourself. Leaving me to learn it this way was hurtful, and it was unfair.

You live in Calgary. I know the building is not part of your everyday life the way it is part of mine. But every morning, I open that door. I have been running my bakery there for thirty-one years. I have six employees whose jobs matter, and clients who have been coming to me for decades. This is how I earn my living. It is how other people earn theirs, too.

You may think I am being sentimental because it was Papa’s building. Of course I am sentimental about it. Papa bought that three-storey building on rue Saint-Hubert in 1979. The bakery downstairs, the two apartments upstairs—we both know that place. Do you remember how much you loved it when he let you sleep in the flour sacks room in the back? You have your own memories there, even if you have been away a long time.

But I need you to hear the business part of this, too. I cannot pick up thirty-one years of work and move it somewhere else as if nothing has happened. A bakery is not just a name on a door. There is the location, the equipment, the people who know where to find us, and all the work that has gone into keeping it going.

My lease ends on April 30, 2027. I do not know what a buyer would plan to do. That is exactly what frightens me. If a developer wants to tear the place down, turn it into condos, or eventually charge rent I cannot afford, what happens to the bakery? I cannot survive having my rent doubled. These are not small worries that I can put aside while you deal with an agent.

I have paid my rent to the estate—$2,400 every month—and I have never been late once. In 2019, I paid $38,000 for the new roof out of my own pocket. That roof was for the whole building, not only the bakery. We need to discuss that money as part of any arrangement between us. I cannot accept it simply being forgotten.

And I already told you I wanted to buy your half. We spoke about it by phone in September. I told you the caisse had pre-approved me for $410,000. This was a serious proposal, Denis. I had taken steps to see what I could afford because I wanted a solution that would let you sell your share and let me keep the bakery.

I understand that $410,000 is not half of the asking price on that listing. I am not pretending that we have agreed on a value or that the financing settles everything. But surely the next step was a conversation with me. We could have discussed the value, the roof payment, what you need, what I can manage, and whether there is a way to make it work. Instead, I found the building advertised online.

I am not asking you to forget that you own half. If you need the money, tell me. If you do not want to own property here anymore, tell me. I can listen to things I do not like hearing. What I cannot do is have a proper conversation with you if you make decisions behind my back.

Here is what I am asking you to do now: take the building off the market this week so we can talk. Tell the agent that I have not agreed to this process, and that no one is to arrive at the bakery for photographs or visits without arranging it with me beforehand.

If you will not take it off the market, then at the very least give me the first opportunity to buy your half before proceeding with anyone else. A real opportunity, with the price and terms clearly laid out and enough time to speak with the caisse and get advice. Not a last-minute call when everything is already decided.

Please call me this week. I want to hear from you directly, by phone. I do not want to deal with this through text messages from your wife. This is not a criticism of her. You are my brother, we own this building together, and this conversation needs to be between us.

I love you. I am very angry with you, and right now I feel betrayed, but I do not want to lose my brother over this. I also cannot stay quiet and risk losing the business I have spent thirty-one years building.

You told me we would decide together. I am asking you to keep that promise. Call me, and give us a chance to sort this out before it goes any further.
